children.value: Rules noticed by the model assigned in the model comparison:

Condition differences in the yes/no answers were tested with χ² tests over the three conditions and with Fisher’s exact test of C3 against C1 and C2. The aversiveness ratings of the two halves, their mean and their change (second minus first half) were modelled with linear models with the two planned contrasts (C3 versus C1 and C2, C2 versus C1) and heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) standard errors; the change was also tested against zero (Wilcoxon). Each of the ten questionnaire totals (z-scored) was related to the answers in models adjusted for condition (logistic regression for “rules noticed”, linear models with HC3 for the ratings), and in a second model with the interaction of the questionnaire with the two contrasts; p-values were corrected with the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure across the five core questionnaires (STICSA state, STICSA trait, IU, BDI-II, OCI) and, separately, across the five further questionnaires, for each outcome and term (q). Because only 8 participants found the instructions unclear, this answer was compared between groups with Mann–Whitney tests. “Rules noticed” was related to behavioural measures and parameters (difference between participants who answered yes and no, in SD of the measure, adjusted for condition; BH across the 13 measures).

The share of participants who reported noticing rules (C1, 16 of 31; C2, 24 of 33; C3, 12 of 22; χ² p = .18), who found the instructions clear (27, 30 and 21; p = .59) and who had consumed caffeine on the day of the session (16, 13 and 11; p = .58) did not differ between conditions. The aversiveness of the task did not differ between conditions (median of both halves 52, 51 and 49; C3 versus C1 and C2, p = .84; C2 versus C1, p = .80), and it did not change from the first to the second half, overall (median change 0.0; 39 participants rated the second half as more aversive, 41 as less aversive, 6 as equal; Wilcoxon p = .65) or in any condition (all p ≥ .39).

Only 12 of the 22 participants in C3, who had been told the rules, answered that they had noticed rules. These participants probably read the question as asking whether they had discovered rules themselves. In C3, the answer therefore does not measure the same as in C1 and C2.

No questionnaire was associated with the report of noticed rules (all q ≥ .39), with the clarity of the instructions (all p ≥ .10) or, across conditions, with the mean or the change of the aversiveness (all q ≥ .44).

The association of the questionnaires with the change of the aversiveness depended on condition (interaction of the questionnaire with the contrast C3 versus C1 and C2) for IU (q = .006), STICSA state anxiety (q = .017) and OCI (q = .037), and among the further questionnaires for PCL-5 (q = .006) and ERS (q = .047). In C3, higher scores were associated with a more aversive first half and a stronger decrease of the aversiveness in the second half (change per SD of the questionnaire: IU −20.4 points, p < .001; PCL-5 −26.7, p < .001; STICSA state −17.9, p = .001; first half: IU +14.5, p < .001; PCL-5 +12.0, p = .011), whereas the slopes in C1 and C2 were between −5 and +10 points (

). A change score depends in part on its starting value, so that part of this association can reflect regression to the mean; the association with the first half alone was significant for IU and PCL-5. The estimates in C3 rest on 21 participants.

children.label: Cross-cue transfer and the learned cue offset

children.value: The larger |I_e| of participants who noticed rules led to a closer look at the measure. |I_e| is the angular deviation of the first placement for the second colour cue after an episode transition from the placement that full transfer of the transition would predict, that is, from the previous placement for this cue rotated by 120° (0° = full transfer; random placement gives 90° on average).

(a) Placement of the first trial of the second colour cue after each episode transition: full transfer (the new direction of this cue), no transfer (the previous direction of this cue), the new or previous direction of the other cue, or elsewhere (none of these within 25°). C1 and C2 are split by the learned cue offset (cue sensitivity above or below 0.5). (b) Mean |I_e| per participant; bars, medians; dashed line, 90°.

In C1 and C2, the participants who had not learned the cue offset (cue sensitivity ≤ 0.5; 22 participants) placed the nets for the second cue most often at the new direction of the first cue (43 % of transitions), which they treat as the same direction. These placements give |I_e| of about 51°, because the direction of the first cue lies 70° from the full-transfer direction of the second cue, and the mean |I_e| of this group (80°) is therefore below 90° without any cue-specific transfer. The participants who had learned the cue offset (42 participants) kept the second cue most often at its previous direction (44 %, |I_e| about 121°), which gives a mean |I_e| above 90° (104°). In C3, 37 % of the placements showed full transfer (mean |I_e| 75°). Of the C1 and C2 participants who reported noticing rules, 32 of 42 had learned the cue offset, against 8 of 22 of those who did not report it. Across participants, |I_e| increased with cue sensitivity (37° per unit, adjusted for condition, p < .001).

In C1 and C2, |I_e| therefore mixes two strategies, treating both cues as one direction and treating them as two independent directions, and values around 90° do not indicate random placement. The difference between C3 and the other conditions (section 2.1.4 of the results chapter) is carried by the share of full transfer (C1, 7 %; C2, 11 %; C3, 36 % of transitions per participant on average). For the questionnaire associations of |I_e| (Model D), the association with OCI arose from a higher share of placements at the previous direction of the second cue (+0.066 per SD, p = .008) and a lower share at the new direction of the first cue (−0.057, p = .012), not from a lower share of full transfer (p = .19); adjusted for cue sensitivity, it was weaker (from 6.8° to 5.0° per SD, p = .073).
